\title{Documenting Possible Gaps, Counterexamples, and Formalization Deviations}
\author{}
\date{2026-04-29}

\begin{document}
\maketitle

\section{Purpose}

When a formalization relies on a cited mathematical source, the cited source
should remain intact.  It is a source, not an errata file.  If a possible gap,
missing hypothesis, incorrect numerical constant, or other mathematical
discrepancy is found, the matter should be recorded in a separate LaTeX note.
In this repository such notes live under \path{docs/paper-gaps/}.  The same
principle applies when the formal development has already diverged from the
cited source, for instance by changing a statement so that it compiles, or by
using a different mathematical route because an available formal-library theorem
has a slightly different form.  Such a note is a mathematical note first, and a
record of the formalization second: it should be readable by a mathematician or
mathematical physicist who has not followed the issue discussion.

The note should isolate the mathematical mechanism.  It should say what the
cited source asserts, what the cited results actually imply, where a term or
hypothesis is lost, and what statement the formal development proves instead.
If the formal proof takes a different route, the note should explain the
replacement argument and the hypotheses on which it rests.  This is especially
important when the proof uses a theorem, construction, or convention from
Mathlib which is not part of the cited argument.  In that case the note should
state the Mathlib result in ordinary mathematical language, explain how it is
specialized to the notation of the paper, and compare its hypotheses and
conclusion with the step it replaces.  It should not merely say that \Lean{} did
not accept a proof, that the modified proof compiles, or that a named library
lemma was applied.

The documents in this directory should themselves follow this standard.  A
policy or template which reads like a checklist will tend to produce checklist
notes; the examples and templates should therefore be written as mathematical
prose.

\section{Concision and Readability}

A paper-gap note should be short enough that a reader can understand the issue
in one sitting.  The first page should answer four questions: what the source
uses, how hard the remaining formal work is, what the formalization or audit
checked, and what the current verdict is.  Begin with a short
\emph{At a glance} section when the note concerns an open or recently resolved
formalization task.  That section should estimate the difficulty, the rough
implementation weight, the split between Mathlib reuse and project-local work,
and the key Mathlib APIs or modules.  Use honest ranges, not false precision.

The \emph{Key theorem forms} section should be Section~2, immediately after
\emph{At a glance}.  Put the theorem forms before the source details so the
reader knows what the formalization is aiming to prove.  After that, keep the
source assertion, the mechanism being checked, the blueprint/formal comparison,
and the conclusion.  Use more sections only when a counterexample or long
derivation genuinely needs room.

Keep background to the minimum needed for the local point.  Prefer one clear
special case over a general restatement of the surrounding theorem.  Use displayed
equations for the source assertion, the key calculation, and the theorem forms;
avoid displays for traceability data, declaration names, or long lists.  The
blueprint/formal comparison should be compact and should not repeat the theorem
forms.  The section ``Form of the Note'' below specifies where traceability data
belongs; the body should read as mathematical prose, not as a log.

If the verdict is that there is no mathematical discrepancy, say so plainly and
stop.  Keep the conclusion highly compact, normally under twenty source lines.
If the only remaining work is an implementation task, name it briefly and link
the issue or pull request in a footnote.

\section{When the Investigation Starts}

The investigation starts when the obstruction appears to be mathematical rather
than merely formal.  No final judgement is needed at this stage.  It is enough
that, after reading the relevant source and attempting the corresponding formal
statement, the proof seems to require a different scalar, an additional
hypothesis, a different tensor placement, a distinction between two objects which
the prose identifies, or an auxiliary assertion not supplied by the cited
argument.

The same investigation should also start when such a deviation is discovered
after the fact.  If the existing formal development or informal blueprint has
already changed the statement, strengthened a hypothesis, weakened a conclusion,
inserted an unadvertised lemma, or replaced the cited proof by a different
formal-library argument, the mathematical change should be documented even if all
relevant files already compile.

At this early stage the purpose is to preserve the question while it is still
local.  The note may later conclude that the matter is only notational, that an
intermediate estimate in the cited source needs a harmless correction, that a
missing hypothesis is genuinely needed, or that no discrepancy remains.  Thus
the trigger is not the severity of the eventual verdict, but the appearance of a
real mismatch between the cited reasoning and the statement that can be
formalized.

A failed tactic search, a missing formal lemma, or an inconvenient coercion is
not enough.  The obstruction must survive translation back into ordinary
mathematics.

Sometimes an investigation uncovers an improvement that is not a discrepancy:
the formalization works correctly, but it could be simplified by using an
existing library, replacing a custom type, or adopting a cleaner proof route.
These are not, by themselves, paper-gap notes.  They are action items.  When
such an improvement is identified, open a GitHub issue or pull request that
describes the proposed change.  If the investigation also produces a paper-gap
note, link the issue or pull request from that note: the note records the
mathematical justification, and the issue or pull request drives the
implementation.

\section{When to Write a Note}

A note should be written once the source argument and the formal proof no longer
match as mathematical arguments.  This includes, for instance, a numerical
estimate whose constant does not follow from the cited lemma, a displayed
conclusion which uses an unstated hypothesis, or a step in which two objects are
identified although they must remain distinct.  In analytic, algebraic,
probabilistic, or quantum arguments, such distinctions may concern the domain of
a map, the placement of a tensor factor, the type of an outcome, the distinction
between a structure and a substructure, or the scalar carried by an approximation
relation.

A note is required when an audit finds that a Lean declaration associated with a
source-labelled statement has acquired an extra non-source hypothesis, such as
bridge, residual, repair, producer, or obligation-structure data.  Such a
declaration is temporary proof debt, not a replacement for the source theorem,
and should not be introduced merely to avoid a \verb|sorry|.  The note must say
plainly that the Lean result is conditional, identify the source-faithful theorem
form that remains to be proved, and give the intended obligation discharger or
removal plan.  The blueprint should not mark the source-labelled statement with
\verb|\leanok| by pointing to this conditional helper.

Changing a Lean theorem away from the statement in
\path{references/ldt-paper/} is strongly discouraged.  A paper-gap note should
not make such a change look routine: it should explain the mathematical
necessity, or else classify the change as proof debt to be removed.

When an existing conditional helper is audited, the first task is to extract any
argument it already contains into source-faithful lemmas.  If the remaining
bridge hypothesis cannot be derived from the paper hypotheses, the formal
development should restore the source theorem statement and record the missing
proof obligation explicitly, rather than retaining the strengthened statement as
though it were the paper theorem.

This requirement is not meant to classify every explicit Lean side condition as
a discrepancy.  Positivity, nonemptiness, decidability, field-model instances,
and denominator nonvanishing hypotheses may be faithful encodings of the domain
in which the paper's theorem is stated.  The note should distinguish such
boundary hypotheses from hypotheses that supply an unproved step of the paper
argument.

A note is also appropriate when the proof becomes formal only after changing an
intermediate scalar, weakening a conclusion, strengthening a hypothesis, or
inserting an additional lemma which is not simply an expansion of the cited
argument.  These are mathematical changes, even when they are harmless for the
final theorem.  It is likewise appropriate when an available formal-library
theorem proves the needed result under a somewhat different formulation from the
cited source.  In that case the note should be deliberately pedagogical.  It
should explain, in ordinary mathematical language, what the replacement result
says, how it is specialized, which hypotheses are new or differently packaged,
and why the resulting statement is a legitimate substitute for the step in the
cited argument.  If the issue remains open after reasonable attempts, the note
should say what has been checked and what remains unknown.

\section{Counterexamples}

If the cited assertion appears to be false, the note should not stop at saying
that the proof cannot be formalized.  It should give the counterexample, or the
smallest relevant part of it, in ordinary mathematical notation.  The example
should be accompanied by enough verification that the reader can see both sides:
the hypotheses of the cited assertion hold, and its conclusion fails.

When feasible, the counterexample should also be formalized in \Lean{}.  This is
especially valuable when the example is finite, algebraic, computational, or
otherwise small enough that the failure can be checked without reproducing the
whole surrounding theory.  The note should then state the mathematical content
of the checked counterexample and identify the corresponding Lean declaration in
a footnote.  The Lean file is not a substitute for the prose: the prose should
still explain why the example refutes the cited assertion.

\section{Revision of a Note}

A paper-gap note may be provisional.  It may begin as soon as the mathematical
obstruction has been isolated well enough to state the question, and it may be
revised as the calculation, the blueprint, or the corresponding \Lean{}
declarations become clearer.  The first version need not know the final
classification, but it should say plainly which mathematical point is known and
which point remains unsettled.

Later revisions should not make the note into a chronological log.  They should
rewrite the document so that it remains a coherent account of the present
mathematical understanding.  If the verdict changes, the conclusion should state
the current verdict; the linked issue or pull request can preserve the earlier
discussion.

\section{Form of the Note}

Each note should stand on its own.  It should give the date, cite the relevant
source article, and provide enough traceability for the reader to locate the
original passage and the project discussion.  GitHub issues and pull requests may
be linked with \verb|\href|, and source files, line ranges, and labels should be
recorded when they help the reader check the claim.  These references should
serve the exposition rather than govern it: the main text should be organized
around the mathematical assertion and its proof.

The note should introduce its notation before using it.  Symbols for
measurements, tensor factors, approximation relations, and error parameters
should be named in prose.  If an approximation relation is state-dependent, the
state should be named, or its defining expression should be given when this can
be done briefly.  Only after the notation is in place should the note state the
assertion in the cited source, using a bibliographic citation such as
\verb|\cite[Section~...]{...}| when the section or chapter is known.

Only the relevant hypotheses should be reproduced.  If the question is a scalar
substitution, a missing term, or a missing hypothesis, the note should not quote
a long unrelated part of the proof.  It should give the cited lemma or
proposition in the special case actually used, then display the calculation or
logical implication in which the discrepancy appears.

Displayed equations should be used with restraint.  They are appropriate for the
source estimate being checked, the cited estimate in the form actually used, and
the calculation where a term or hypothesis appears or disappears.  When a
displayed equation is identified by a source label, the label should appear on
the right of the display, while the surrounding prose refers to the mathematical
assertion itself.  The standard \texttt{amsmath} command \verb|\tag| is the
right mechanism for this; a separate local convention should be introduced only
if the standard mechanism is genuinely insufficient.  For a multi-line aligned
display, tag the individual lines that carry the source information rather than
forcing a long combined label below the equations.  Short
scalar definitions and elementary inequalities should remain inline when the
sentence reads better that way.  As in ordinary mathematical writing, a displayed
formula is part of the surrounding sentence and should be punctuated accordingly.

Bibliographic entries used only by these notes should live in
\path{docs/paper-gaps/references.bib}.  A new note should ordinarily begin from
\path{docs/paper-gaps/template.tex}, which records the common LaTeX preamble,
the local bibliography, and a model for right-hand source labels in displayed
equations.

Blueprint prose cites a note like any other source, with
\verb|\cite{gap:<slug>}|; the bibliography entry in
\path{blueprint/src/references.bib} carries the published URL of the note,
whether the note lives in this repository or in another one.  Lean docstrings
and comments use the repository path form \path{docs/paper-gaps/<slug>.tex}.

The note should then compare the cited source with the informal blueprint, if
there is one, and with the formal statement.  This comparison should be written
in ordinary mathematical prose.  Formal declaration names and source paths should
be supplied only to identify the exact formal statements, and normally belong in
footnotes.

The conclusion should give a verdict.  It may say that there is no discrepancy,
that the matter is only notational, that an intermediate estimate needs a
harmless correction, that a hypothesis is missing, that there is a theorem-level
gap, or that the question remains open.  The classification should reflect the
mathematics, not the amount of formal work required.

\section{Decision Principle}

The formal development should not silently replace the cited assertion by a
different one.  If the formal statement differs from the cited source, the
reason for the difference should be written down.  Conversely, the note should
not overstate the conclusion.  A wrong intermediate scalar is not a fatal gap in
the theorem if the corrected scalar is bounded by the error parameter appearing
in the theorem statement.

\end{document}

     4	/-! # Polynomial decoding for Pauli extraction
     5	
     6	This module provides the Chapter 16 decoder on the Chapter 15 bounded
     7	polynomial representative type.  The generic retained-value decoder and its
     8	specialization to polynomial representatives live in
     9	`Algebra/LowDegreeCodeTheorems`; this module states the corresponding maps on
    10	`Poly P` used in the extraction chapter.
    11	
    12	## References
    13	
    14	The decoder is `def:decoding-map`, blueprint
    15	`blueprint/src/chapter/ch11_qpbt_algebra.tex:445-455`, with the extraction use
    16	at `blueprint/src/chapter/ch16_qpbt_extraction.tex:11-20` and paper
    17	`references/qpbt-paper/14_analysis_of_the_pauli_basis_test.tex:1419-1450`.
    18	The restricted decoder identity and its encoding hypothesis are documented in
    19	`docs/paper-gaps/qpbt_decoding-identity.tex:87-123`.
    20	-/
    21	
    22	open scoped BigOperators
    23	
    24	namespace MIPStarRE.QPBT
    25	
    26	open MIPStarRE.LDT MIPStarRE.LDT.Preliminaries
    27	
    28	/-! ## Representative evaluation and decoding -/
    29	
    30	/-- Evaluate the polynomial representative carried by `Poly P`.
    31	
    32	This is polynomial evaluation on the source's `\ideg_{d,m}(\F_q)` carrier.  It
    33	does not identify representatives that induce the same polynomial function. -/
    34	noncomputable def evalPoly {P : AdmissibleParams} (g : Poly P)
    35	    (x : Fin P.m → PauliScalar P) : PauliScalar P :=
    36	  MvPolynomial.eval x g.1
    37	
    38	/-- Decode a bounded polynomial while retaining only values in `H`.
    39	
    40	This is the `H`-parameterized form of `def:decoding-map`; `decodeAt` remains
    41	the decoding map for arbitrary functions.  The Boolean cube is embedded in
    42	`PauliScalar P` by `cubeEmbed`. -/
    43	noncomputable def decodeOn {P : AdmissibleParams}
    44	    (H : Finset (PauliScalar P)) (g : Poly P) : PauliRegister P :=
    45	  decodeAt H (fun x => evalPoly g x)
    46	
    47	/-- Full-field specialization of `decodeOn` used in Chapter 16.
    48	
    49	The retained-value set is `Finset.univ`, so every field value is kept.  This
    50	choice is the correction recorded in
    51	`docs/paper-gaps/qpbt_decoding-identity.tex:87-123`. -/
    52	noncomputable abbrev decodeOnUniv {P : AdmissibleParams} (g : Poly P) :
    53	    PauliRegister P :=
    54	  decodeOn (Finset.univ : Finset (PauliScalar P)) g
    55	
    56	/-- The full-field decoder `\operatorname{Dec}_{\F_q}` on `Poly P`.
    57	
    58	The map `decodeFqRep` has the same definition on arbitrary polynomial
    59	representatives; `decodeFq` restricts its domain to the bounded-degree class
    60	`Poly P`. -/
    61	noncomputable abbrev decodeFq {P : AdmissibleParams} (g : Poly P) :
    62	    PauliRegister P :=
    63	  decodeOnUniv g
    64	
    65	/-! ## The encoding image -/
    66	
    67	/-- Membership of a multilinear encoding in the bounded representative class.
    68	
    69	The proof that the multilinear encoding has individual degree at most one,
    70	and hence at most `P.d` using `P.hd`, is a named proof obligation.  It is the
    71	degree side-condition implicit in the source's `g_h` construction, not an
    72	extra hypothesis of the decoding identity.  See
    73	`blueprint/src/chapter/ch11_qpbt_algebra.tex:381-401` and paper
    74	`references/qpbt-paper/04_preliminaries.tex:832-897`.
    75	
    76	**Proof obligation:** issue #47 tracks the individual-degree calculation. -/
    77	theorem lowDegreeEncoding_mem_poly {P : AdmissibleParams}
    78	    (h : PauliRegister P) :
    79	    lowDegreeEncoding h ∈
    80	      MIPStarRE.LDT.Preliminaries.polyFunc P.m (PauliScalar P) P.d := by
    81	  sorry
    82	
    83	/-- The multilinear encoding as a bounded polynomial representative.
    84	
    85	The individual-degree bound is supplied by `lowDegreeEncoding_mem_poly`. -/
    86	noncomputable def encodingPoly {P : AdmissibleParams} (h : PauliRegister P) :
    87	    Poly P :=
    88	  ⟨lowDegreeEncoding h, lowDegreeEncoding_mem_poly h⟩
    89	
    90	/-- A `Poly P` outcome is an encoding when its decoder reconstructs the same
    91	underlying polynomial representative.
    92	
    93	This is the explicit support restriction required by the corrected Chapter 16
    94	decoding argument.  It is the `Poly` view of `IsEncodingRep`; no unrestricted
    95	decoder/evaluation identity is asserted.  See
    96	`docs/paper-gaps/qpbt_decoding-identity.tex:87-123`. -/
    97	def IsEncoding {P : AdmissibleParams} (g : Poly P) : Prop :=
    98	  lowDegreeEncoding (decodeFq g) = g.1
    99	
   100	/-! ## Decoder companions -/
   101	
   102	/-- Linearity of the full-field decoder on bounded representatives.
   103	
   104	This is the linearity used in the source's regrouping calculation at paper
   105	`14_analysis_of_the_pauli_basis_test.tex:1442-1450` and blueprint
   106	`ch16_qpbt_extraction.tex:11-20`.  It is a proof obligation; it does not
   107	assert evaluation equality for non-encoding representatives.  See
   108	`docs/paper-gaps/qpbt_decoding-identity.tex:87-123`.
   109	
   110	**Proof obligation:** issue #47 tracks the regrouping calculation. -/
   111	theorem decodeFq_add {P : AdmissibleParams} (g h : Poly P) :
   112	    decodeFq (g + h) = decodeFq g + decodeFq h := by
   113	  sorry
   114	
   115	/-- Scalar linearity of the full-field decoder on bounded representatives.
   116	
   117	This companion has the same source and proof-gap status as `decodeFq_add` and
   118	does not strengthen the restricted decoder identity.  See
   119	`docs/paper-gaps/qpbt_decoding-identity.tex:87-123`.
   120	
   121	**Proof obligation:** issue #47 tracks scalar linearity. -/
   122	theorem decodeFq_smul {P : AdmissibleParams} (c : PauliScalar P) (g : Poly P) :
   123	    decodeFq (c • g) = c • decodeFq g := by
   124	  sorry
   125	
   126	/-- The full-field decoder is a left inverse to `encodingPoly`.
   127	
   128	This is the source identity `\operatorname{Dec}(g_h)=h` from
   129	`references/qpbt-paper/14_analysis_of_the_pauli_basis_test.tex:1805-1822`.
   130	The degree proof is separated into `lowDegreeEncoding_mem_poly`; no additional
   131	encoding or interpolation hypothesis is introduced.  See
   132	`docs/paper-gaps/qpbt_decoding-identity.tex:87-123`.
   133	
   134	**Proof obligation:** issue #47 tracks the decoder/encoding calculation. -/
   135	theorem decodeFq_lowDegreeEncoding {P : AdmissibleParams}
   136	    (h : PauliRegister P) :
   137	    decodeFq (encodingPoly h) = h := by
   138	  sorry
   139	
   140	/-- Decoder/evaluation agreement for an encoding representative only.
   141	
   142	The hypothesis `hg : IsEncoding g` is mandatory.  For a general bounded
   143	polynomial, Boolean-cube values determine its multilinear interpolant, which
   144	need not equal the original representative.  This is the corrected form of
   145	the source step at
   146	`references/qpbt-paper/14_analysis_of_the_pauli_basis_test.tex:1483-1492`;
   147	see `docs/paper-gaps/qpbt_decoding-identity.tex:87-123`.
   148	
   149	**Proof obligation:** issue #47 tracks the restricted evaluation calculation. -/
   150	theorem decodeFq_dotProduct_indicatorVec {P : AdmissibleParams}
   151	    {g : Poly P} (hg : IsEncoding g) (x : Fin P.m → PauliScalar P) :
   152	    dotProduct (decodeFq g) (indicatorVec x) = evalPoly g x := by
   153	  sorry
   154	
   155	end MIPStarRE.QPBT

     3	/-!
     4	# Extraction foundations
     5	
     6	This module defines the register identifications used to pull the Pauli
     7	measurements apart. It retains the distinct local spaces of a
     8	heterogeneous strategy, coarse-grains the generalized Pauli projectors by a
     9	dot product, and records the state and error expressions needed by the later
    10	extraction witness.
    11	
    12	The binary phases use the existing `phaseSign`; the fixed field basis remains
    13	the basis stored in `P.model` and is not re-quantified here.
    14	
    15	## References
    16	
    17	The Pauli dot-product projectors formalize `def:tau-dot-product-projector` in
    18	`blueprint/src/chapter/ch16_qpbt_extraction.tex:46-53`, from
    19	`references/qpbt-paper/14_analysis_of_the_pauli_basis_test.tex:1426-1429`.
    20	The register and state helpers support `def:tilde-m-measurement`,
    21	`def:v-swap-unitary`, and `lem:qld-unitary`, from paper lines 1429-1435 and
    22	1666-1713 and blueprint lines 55-62 and 203-260.
    23	-/
    24	
    25	open scoped BigOperators Matrix
    26	
    27	namespace MIPStarRE.QPBT
    28	
    29	open MIPStarRE.Quantum
    30	
    31	noncomputable section
    32	
    33	/-! ## Heterogeneous extraction registers -/
    34	
    35	/-- One player's registers after adjoining the two generalized-Pauli
    36	registers: `AA'A''` or `BB'B''`. This identifies the register order and spaces for
    37	paper `14_analysis_of_the_pauli_basis_test.tex:1429-1435,1687-1713` and
    38	blueprint `ch16_qpbt_extraction.tex:55-62,203-230`. -/
    39	abbrev ExtractionBlock (P : AdmissibleParams) (ι : Type*) :=
    40	  (ι × PauliRegister P) × PauliRegister P
    41	
    42	/-- The two heterogeneous extraction blocks in the order
    43	`AA'A'' | BB'B''`. This is the block presentation of the existing `SixReg`
    44	space used in `lem:qld-unitary`, blueprint
    45	`ch16_qpbt_extraction.tex:245-260`, paper
    46	`14_analysis_of_the_pauli_basis_test.tex:1666-1685`. -/
    47	abbrev ExtractionRegisters (P : AdmissibleParams) (ιA ιB : Type*) :=
    48	  ExtractionBlock P ιA × ExtractionBlock P ιB
    49	
    50	/-- The auxiliary registers `AA'BB'` occurring before the extracted EPR
    51	factor in `lem:qld-unitary`, blueprint `ch16_qpbt_extraction.tex:245-260`,
    52	paper `14_analysis_of_the_pauli_basis_test.tex:1666-1685`. -/
    53	abbrev ExtractionAuxRegisters (P : AdmissibleParams) (ιA ιB : Type*) :=
    54	  (ιA × PauliRegister P) × (ιB × PauliRegister P)
    55	
    56	/-- Reassociate the six-register order with the two extraction blocks.
    57	This equivalence identifies the register order in paper
    58	`14_analysis_of_the_pauli_basis_test.tex:1429-1435,1687-1713`. -/
    59	def sixRegExtractionEquiv (P : AdmissibleParams) (ιA ιB : Type*) :
    60	    SixReg P ιA ιB ≃ ExtractionRegisters P ιA ιB where
    61	  toFun p := (((p.1.1, p.1.2.1), p.1.2.2),
    62	    ((p.2.1, p.2.2.1), p.2.2.2))
    63	  invFun p := ((p.1.1.1, (p.1.1.2, p.1.2)),
    64	    (p.2.1.1, (p.2.1.2, p.2.2)))
    65	  left_inv p := by cases p; rfl
    66	  right_inv p := by cases p; rfl
    67	
    68	/-- Shuffle `AA'BB' | A''B''` into the six-register order. This equivalence
    69	places the ideal state in the order used in `lem:qld-unitary`, blueprint
    70	`ch16_qpbt_extraction.tex:245-260`, paper
    71	`14_analysis_of_the_pauli_basis_test.tex:1666-1685`. -/
    72	def extractionIdealShuffle (P : AdmissibleParams) (ιA ιB : Type*) :
    73	    (ExtractionAuxRegisters P ιA ιB ×
    74	      (PauliRegister P × PauliRegister P)) ≃ SixReg P ιA ιB where
    75	  toFun p := ((p.1.1.1, (p.1.1.2, p.2.1)),
    76	    (p.1.2.1, (p.1.2.2, p.2.2)))
    77	  invFun p := (((p.1.1, p.1.2.1), (p.2.1, p.2.2.1)),
    78	    (p.1.2.2, p.2.2.2))
    79	  left_inv p := by cases p; rfl
    80	  right_inv p := by cases p; rfl

    82	namespace ProjectiveSetting
    83	
    84	variable {P : AdmissibleParams} {ε : ℝ}
    85	
    86	/-- Place an operator on one complete extraction block, with the identity on
    87	the other player's block, as in the side-qualified operators of paper
    88	`14_analysis_of_the_pauli_basis_test.tex:1429-1435,1687-1713`. -/
    89	noncomputable def placeSide (S : ProjectiveSetting P ε) (side : PlayerSide)
    90	    (O : Op (ExtractionBlock P (S.LocalSpace side))) :
    91	    Op (SixReg P S.toStrategy.ιA S.toStrategy.ιB) := by
    92	  cases side with
    93	  | alice =>
    94	      exact reindexOp
    95	        (sixRegExtractionEquiv P S.toStrategy.ιA S.toStrategy.ιB)
    96	        (heteroKron O 1)
    97	  | bob =>
    98	      exact reindexOp
    99	        (sixRegExtractionEquiv P S.toStrategy.ιA S.toStrategy.ιB)
   100	        (heteroKron 1 O)
   101	
   102	/-- Lift an operator on a player's original strategy register to that player's
   103	full extraction block. This places the Pauli and point measurements appearing
   104	in `lem:qld-construct-the-paulis` and `lem:qld-unitary`, blueprint
   105	`ch16_qpbt_extraction.tex:105-124,245-260`. -/
   106	noncomputable def onPlayer (S : ProjectiveSetting P ε) (side : PlayerSide)
   107	    (O : Op (S.LocalSpace side)) :
   108	    Op (ExtractionBlock P (S.LocalSpace side)) :=
   109	  heteroKron (heteroKron O 1) 1
   110	
   111	/-- Place an operator on the original strategy register of the selected
   112	player. This is the player-side placement used in `lem:qld-unitary`,
   113	blueprint `ch16_qpbt_extraction.tex:245-260`. -/
   114	noncomputable def placePlayer (S : ProjectiveSetting P ε) (side : PlayerSide)
   115	    (O : Op (S.LocalSpace side)) :
   116	    Op (SixReg P S.toStrategy.ιA S.toStrategy.ιB) := by
   117	  cases side with
   118	  | alice => exact S.place .AA' (heteroKron O 1)
   119	  | bob => exact S.place .BB' (heteroKron O 1)
   120	
   121	/-- Place an operator on the selected extracted register `A''` or `B''`.
   122	The unused strategy register in the crossed placement is assigned the
   123	identity. This is the placement of the ideal Pauli operators in
   124	`lem:qld-unitary`, blueprint `ch16_qpbt_extraction.tex:245-260`, paper

   126	noncomputable def placeExtractedRegister (S : ProjectiveSetting P ε)
   127	    (side : PlayerSide) (O : Op (PauliRegister P)) :
   128	    Op (SixReg P S.toStrategy.ιA S.toStrategy.ιB) := by

   130	  | alice =>
   131	      exact S.place .BA'' (heteroKron (1 : Op S.toStrategy.ιB) O)
   132	  | bob =>
   133	      exact S.place .AB'' (heteroKron (1 : Op S.toStrategy.ιA) O)

   149	`14_analysis_of_the_pauli_basis_test.tex:1666-1685`. -/

   173	/-! ## Coarse-grained Pauli projectors -/

   178	`ch16_qpbt_extraction.tex:46-53`. -/
   179	noncomputable def bracketOp {α β ι : Type*} [Fintype α] [DecidableEq β]
   180	    (N : α → Op ι) (f : α → β) (b : β) : Op ι :=
   181	  ∑ a ∈ Finset.univ.filter (fun a => f a = b), N a
   182	
   183	/-- The effect of a postprocessed measurement is the corresponding
   184	coarse-grained operator sum. This equality is used by `def:bracket` and
   185	`def:tau-dot-product-projector`, blueprint
   186	`ch12_qpbt_games.tex:8-26` and `ch16_qpbt_extraction.tex:46-53`. -/

   188	    [Fintype α] [DecidableEq α] [Fintype β] [DecidableEq β]
   189	    [Fintype ι] [DecidableEq ι] (M : Measurement α ι) (f : α → β) (b : β) :
   190	    (M.postprocess f).effect b = bracketOp M.effect f b :=
   191	  rfl
   192	
   193	/-- The projector obtained by measuring in basis `W` and retaining outcomes
   194	whose dot product with `u` is `a`. This is Equation `eq:def-tauwu` in

   196	`ch16_qpbt_extraction.tex:46-53`, paper
   197	`14_analysis_of_the_pauli_basis_test.tex:1426-1429`. -/

   199	    (u : PauliRegister P) (a : PauliScalar P) : Op (PauliRegister P) :=
   200	  bracketOp (pauliProj W) (fun h => dotProduct h u) a
   201	
   202	/-- Each dot-product coarse-graining is a projector, as asserted in
   203	`def:tau-dot-product-projector`, blueprint
   204	`ch16_qpbt_extraction.tex:46-53`, paper
   205	`14_analysis_of_the_pauli_basis_test.tex:1426-1429`.
   206

   208	calculation. -/

   210	    (u : PauliRegister P) (a : PauliScalar P) :
   211	    IsProj (tauDotProj W u a) := by
   212	  sorry
   213	
   214	/-- For fixed `W` and `u`, the dot-product projectors sum to the identity.
   215	This is the completeness assertion of `def:tau-dot-product-projector`,
   216	blueprint `ch16_qpbt_extraction.tex:46-53`, paper
   217	`14_analysis_of_the_pauli_basis_test.tex:1426-1429`.
   218	
   219	**Proof obligation:** issue #47 tracks completeness of the generalized-Pauli
   220	projector family. -/
   221	theorem sum_tauDotProj_eq_one {P : AdmissibleParams} (W : PauliKind)
   222	    (u : PauliRegister P) :
   223	    ∑ a : PauliScalar P, tauDotProj W u a = 1 := by
   224	  sorry
   225	
   226	/-! ## Conjugation and extraction error -/
   227	
   228	/-- Conjugation of an operator by a square matrix, as used in the exact
   229	conjugation equations in `lem:v-swap-conjugation`, blueprint
   230	`ch16_qpbt_extraction.tex:216-230`, paper
   231	`14_analysis_of_the_pauli_basis_test.tex:1687-1713`. -/
   232	noncomputable def conjBy {ι : Type*} [Fintype ι]
   233	    (V N : Op ι) : Op ι :=
   234	  V * N * Vᴴ
   235	
   236	/-- The common error scale for constructing the pulled-apart measurements from
   237	a global polynomial-pair witness. Here `deltaG` is its consistency error. The
   238	remaining terms record the point-measurement transfer
   239	and the Schwartz--Zippel loss; when `0 ≤ epsilon ≤ 1`, `sqrt epsilon` also
   240	dominates terms of order `epsilon`.
   241	
   242	This makes explicit the enlargement of the error called `deltaS` in
   243	`lem:qld-construct-the-paulis`, blueprint
   244	`ch16_qpbt_extraction.tex:120-196`, paper
   245	`14_analysis_of_the_pauli_basis_test.tex:1458-1605`. -/
   246	noncomputable def deltaConstructPaulis (C epsilon deltaG : ℝ)
   247	    (m d q : ℕ) : ℝ :=
   248	  C * (deltaG + Real.sqrt epsilon +
   249	    ((m * d : ℕ) : ℝ) / (q : ℝ))
   250	
   251	/-- The explicit extraction scale
   252	`C * (deltaS^(1/4) + md/q)` from `lem:qld-unitary`, blueprint
   253	`ch16_qpbt_extraction.tex:245-260`, paper
   254	`14_analysis_of_the_pauli_basis_test.tex:1666-1685`. -/
   255	noncomputable def deltaExtract (C deltaS : ℝ) (m d q : ℕ) : ℝ :=
   256	  C * (Real.rpow deltaS (1 / 4 : ℝ) + ((m * d : ℕ) : ℝ) / (q : ℝ))
   257	
   258	end
   259	
   260	end MIPStarRE.QPBT

  1666	 The next lemma shows that we can construct local unitaries $V_A,V_B$ from the measurements $\hat{S}$  such that the shared state $\ket{\hat{\psi}}$ is close to $\ket{\aux} \otimes \ket{\EPR_q}^{\otimes \nqubits}$ for some state $\ket{\aux}$, and the observables $\tilde{W}^j(\tilde{u})$ are mapped to Pauli observables $\tau^W(e_j \tilde{u})$ acting on $\ket{\EPR_q}^{\otimes \nqubits}$.   1669	\begin{lemma}
  1670	\label{lem:qld-unitary}
  1671	There exists a function $\delta_\qld(\eps,m,d,q) = O(\delta_S^{1/4} + md/q)$ (where $\delta_S$ is defined in \Cref{lem:qld-4-7}) and unitaries $V_\alice$ acting on registers $\alice \alice' \alice''$ and $V_\bob$ acting on $\bob \bob' \bob''$ such that 
  1672	\begin{enumerate}
  1673		\item There exists a state $\ket{\aux}$ on registers $\alice \alice' \bob \bob'$ such that
  1674		\[
  1675			\left \| V_\alice \otimes V_\bob \ket{\hat{\psi}}_{\alice \alice' \alice'' \bob \bob' \bob''} - \ket{\aux}_{\alice \alice' \bob \bob'} \otimes \ket{\EPR_q}^{\otimes \nqubits}_{\alice'' \bob''} \right \|^2 \leq \delta_\qld.
  1676		\]
  1677		
  1678		\item For all $W \in \{X,Z\}, h \in \F_q^\nqubits$
  1679		\begin{align*}
  1680			V_\alice \, \Big(M^{(\Pauli,W)}_h \Big)_{\alice} \, V_\alice^\dagger &\approx_{\delta_\qld} \Id_{\alice \alice'} \otimes (\tau^W_h)_{\alice''} \\
  1681			 V_\bob \, \Big(M^{(\Pauli,W)}_h  \Big)_{\bob}\, V_\bob^\dagger &\approx_{\delta_\qld} \Id_{\bob \bob'} \otimes (\tau^W_h)_{\bob''}
  1682		\end{align*}
  1683		where the $\approx$ statements hold with respect to the state $\ket{\aux}_{\alice \alice' \bob \bob'} \otimes \ket{\EPR_q}^{\otimes \nqubits}_{\alice'' \bob''}$. 
  1684	\end{enumerate}
  1685	\end{lemma}

  1687	\begin{proof}
  1688	
  1689	Define the linear map
  1690	\[
  1691		V_\alice = \sum_{g_X,g_Z} (\hat{S}_{g_X,g_Z})_{\alice \alice'} \otimes (\tau^X(\coded(g_Z)) \tau^Z(\coded(g_X)))_{\alice ''}\;,
  1692	\]
  1693	where the $\tau^X(\cdot),\tau^Z(\cdot)$ act on $(\C^q)^{\otimes \nqubits}$. (Also note that the argument of $\tau^X$ is $\coded(g_Z)$ and the argument of $\tau^Z$ is $\coded(g_X)$.) We verify the unitarity of $V_\alice$:
  1694	\begin{align*}
  1695		V_\alice V_\alice^\dagger &= \sum_{g_X,g_Z} (\hat{S}_{g_X,g_Z})_{\alice \alice'} \otimes (\tau^X(\coded(g_Z)) \tau^Z(\coded(g_X)) \tau^Z(\coded(g_X)) \tau^X(\coded(g_Z)) )_{\alice ''} \\
  1696		&= \sum_{g_X,g_Z} (\hat{S}_{g_X,g_Z})_{\alice \alice'} \otimes \Id_{\alice ''} \\
  1697		&= \Id_{\alice \alice' \alice''}
  1698	\end{align*}
  1699	where in the first line we used that the measurement $\{ \hat{S}_{g_\xpt,g_\zpt} \}$  is projective and in the second line we used that the $\tau^Z$ and $\tau^X$ observables are self-inverse. The unitary $V_\bob$ is defined analogously.
  1700	
  1701	Let $\{e_j\}_{j \in \{1,\ldots,t\}}$ denote the self-dual basis for $\F_q$ over $\F_2$ specified in \Cref{sec:subfields}, and let $\tilde{W}^j$ be the observables introduced in~\eqref{eq:def-tildewj}. Conjugating the observable $\tilde{W}^j$ acting on the registers $\alice \alice' \alice''$ by the unitary $V_\alice$ we get
  1702	\begin{align*}
  1703		&V_\alice \, \tilde{W}^j(\tilde{u}) \, V_\alice^\dagger \\
  1704	  =& \sum_{g_X, g_Z} (-1)^{\tr( e_j(\coded(g_W) \cdot \tilde{u}))} \Big( \hat{S}_{g_X,g_Z}  \Big)_{\alice \alice'} \otimes \Big ( \tau^X(\coded(g_Z)) \tau^Z(\coded(g_X)) \tau^W(e_j \tilde{u}) \\
  1705	  &\hspace{24em}\tau^Z(\coded(g_X))^\dagger \tau^X(\coded(g_Z))^\dagger \Big)_{\alice ''} \\
  1706		 =& \sum_{g_X, g_Z} \Big( \hat{S}_{g_X,g_Z}  \Big)_{\alice \alice'} \otimes \Big ( \tau^W(e_j \tilde{u}) \Big)_{\alice ''} \\
  1707		 =& \Id_{\alice \alice'} \otimes \Big( \tau^W(e_j \tilde{u}) \Big)_{\alice ''}\;,
  1708	\end{align*}
  1709	where in the third line we used the (anti-)commutation relation
  1710	\[
  1711		\tau^X(\coded(g_Z)) \tau^Z(\coded(g_X)) \tau^W(e_j \tilde{u}) = (-1)^{\tr( e_j(\coded(g_W) \cdot \tilde{u}))} \tau^W(e_j \tilde{u}) \tau^X(\coded(g_Z)) \tau^Z(\coded(g_X)) \;.

  1714	
  1715	Next, from the self-consistency property of the observables $\tilde{W}^j$ specified in \Cref{lem:qld-construct-the-paulis} we get that for $W \in \{X,Z\}$,
  1716	\[
  1717		\E_{j \in \{1,\ldots,t\}} \E_{\tilde{u} \in \F_q^\nqubits} \bra{\hat{\psi}} \left ( \tilde{W}^j(\tilde{u}) \otimes \Id - \Id \otimes \tilde{W}^j(\tilde{u}) \right)^\dagger \left ( \tilde{W}^j(\tilde{u}) \otimes \Id - \Id \otimes \tilde{W}^j(\tilde{u}) \right) \ket{\hat{\psi}} \leq \delta_S\;,

  1719	which, since $\tilde{W}^j$ is Hermitian, is equivalent to
  1720	\begin{equation}
  1721	\label{eq:qld-unitary-1}

  1723	\end{equation}
  1724	Let $\ket{\vartheta} = V_\alice \otimes V_\bob \ket{\hat{\psi}}$, and for $W \in \{X,Z\}$ define the operator
  1725	\begin{align*}
  1726		H_W &= \E_{j \in \{1,\ldots,t\}} \E_{\tilde{u} \in \F_q^\nqubits} \tau^W(e_j \tilde{u}) \otimes \tau^W(e_j \tilde{u}) \\
  1727			&= \E_{j \in \{1,\ldots,t\}} \Big ( \E_{s \in \F_q} \tau^W(e_j s) \otimes \tau^W(e_j s) \Big)^{\otimes \nqubits} \\

  1731	\[

  1733	\]
  1734	for $W \in \{X,Z\}$. 
  1735	
  1736	Observe that
  1737	\begin{align*}
  1738		\E_{s,s'} \tau^X(s) \tau^Z(s') \otimes \tau^X(s) \tau^Z(s') &= \E_{s,s'} \sum_{a,b \in \F_q} (-1)^{\tr(as')} \ketbra{a+s}{a} \otimes (-1)^{\tr(bs')} \ketbra{b+s}{b} \\
  1739		&= \E_{s} \sum_{a\in \F_q} \ketbra{a+s}{a} \otimes \ketbra{a+s}{a} \\

  1742	where to go from the first to the second line we used \Cref{lem:cancellation}. This implies that $H_X H_Z = \Big ( \E_{s,s' \in \F_q} \tau^X(s)\tau^Z(s') \otimes \tau^X(s)\tau^Z(s') \Big)^{\otimes \nqubits} = \ketbra{\EPR_q}{\EPR_q}^{\otimes \nqubits}$.
  1743	By the triangle inequality, we have
  1744	\[
  1745		\left \| H_X \ket{\vartheta} - H_Z \ket{\vartheta} \right\| \leq \left \| \ket{\vartheta} - H_X \ket{\vartheta} \right\| + \left \| \ket{\vartheta} - H_Z \ket{\vartheta} \right\|\;.
  1746	\]
  1747	Note that for $W \in \{X,Z\}$,
  1748	\[
  1749		\left \| \ket{\vartheta} - H_W \ket{\vartheta} \right\|^2 = 1 - 2\bra{\vartheta} H_W \ket{\vartheta} + \bra{\vartheta} H_W^2 \ket{\vartheta} \leq 2 - 2\bra{\vartheta} H_W \ket{\vartheta} \leq \delta_S\;,
  1750	\]
  1751	where in the inequality we used that $H_W \leq \Id$. Furthermore,
  1752	\begin{align*}
  1753		\bra{\vartheta} H_W^2 \ket{\vartheta} &=\| H_W \ket{\vartheta} \|^2\\
  1754		 &= \| \ket{\vartheta} + (H_W - \Id) \ket{\vartheta} \|^2 \\
  1755		 &\geq (\|\ket{\vartheta}\| - \| (H_W - \Id) \ket{\vartheta} \|)^2 \\
  1756		 &\geq (1 - \delta_S)^2 \\
  1757		 &\geq 1 - 2\delta_S\;. 
  1758	\end{align*}
  1759	Therefore 
  1760	\begin{align*}
  1761	2\sqrt{\delta_S} &\geq \left \| H_X \ket{\vartheta} - H_Z \ket{\vartheta} \right\|^2  \\
  1762	&= \bra{\vartheta} H_X^2 \ket{\vartheta} + \bra{\vartheta} H_Z^2 \ket{\vartheta} - 2\bra{\vartheta} H_X H_Z \ket{\vartheta} \\

  1766	\[

  1769	Define the unnormalized state $\ket{\aux_0}$ on the registers $\alice \alice' \bob \bob'$ as
  1770	\[
  1771		\ket{\aux_0}_{\alice \alice' \bob \bob'} = (\bra{\EPR_q}^{\otimes \nqubits})_{\alice'' \bob''} \cdot \ket{\vartheta}_{\alice \alice' \alice'' \bob \bob' \bob''}
  1772	\]
  1773	and define the normalized state $\ket{\aux} = \frac{1}{\| \, \ket{\aux_0} \, \|} \ket{\aux_0}$.

  1785	We now establish the second item of the lemma. In what follows, all $\simeq$ and $\approx$ statements hold with respect to the state $\ket{\hat{\psi}}$. From \Cref{lem:qld-win-implications} we have the following implications: for all $W \in \{X,Z\}$ and on average over $u \in \F_q^m$,

  1863	\begin{proof}[Proof of \Cref{thm:pauli-appendix}]

   832	\subsection{Polynomials and the low-degree code}
   833	\label{sec:ld-encoding}
   834	
   835	In this section, we introduce some basic definitions about polynomials over finite fields. 
   836	An $m$-variate polynomial $f$ over $\F_q$ is a function of the form
   837	\[
   838		f(x_1,\ldots,x_m) = \sum_{\alpha \in \{0,1,\ldots,q-1\}^m} c_\alpha
   839	  x_1^{\alpha_1} \cdots x_m^{\alpha_m}
   840	\]
   841	where $\{c_\alpha\}$ is a collection of coefficients in $\F_q$.
   842	We say that $f$ has \emph{individual degree (at most) $d$} if $c_\alpha\neq 0$ only if
   843	$\alpha_i \leq d $ for all $1\leq i\leq m$, and that it has \emph{total degree
   844	  (at most) $d$} if $c_\alpha\neq 0$ only if $\sum_i \alpha_i \leq d$.
   845	(Affine) \emph{multilinear} polynomials are polynomials with individual degree
   846	$1$.
   847	
   848	Low-degree polynomials play an important role in this paper.
   849	For one, the classical and quantum low-degree tests of \Cref{sec:ldt} are
   850	nonlocal games that efficiently certify that the players' answers are consistent
   851	with low-degree polynomials.
   852	Low-degree polynomials are also crucial in the probabilistically checkable
   853	proofs (PCP) construction that are used in ``answer reduction'' transformation
   854	(\Cref{sec:ans}).
   855	
   856	We recall the Schwartz-Zippel lemma: 
   857	
   858	\begin{lemma}[Schwartz-Zippel lemma~\cite{Sch80,Zip79}]
   859	  \label{lem:schwartz-zippel}
   860	  Let $f, g: \F_q^m \to \F_q$ be two unequal polynomials with total degree at most $d$. Then
   861	  \begin{equation*}
   862	    \Pr_{x \sim \F_q^m}[f(x) = g(x)] \leq d/q\;.
   863	  \end{equation*}
   864	\end{lemma}
   865	
   866	
   867	\paragraph{The low-degree code.}
   868	The Schwartz-Zippel lemma implies that the set of low-degree polynomials form an
   869	error-correcting code with good distance, which we call the \emph{low-degree
   870	  code}.\footnote{It is also known as the \emph{generalized Reed-Muller code} in
   871	  the coding theory literature.}
   872	
   873	Fix an integer $m \in \N$ and let $M = 2^m$.
   874	For every $y \in \{0,1\}^m$ define the following $m$-variate multilinear
   875	polynomial over $\F_q$:
   876	\[
   877		\ind_{m,y}(x) = \prod_{i: y_i = 1} x_i \cdot \prod_{i: y_i = 0} (1 - x_i) \;.
   878	\]
   879	Here, we identify $\{0,1\}$ as a subset of $\F_q$.
   880	Notice that, when restricted to the subcube $\{0,1\}^m$, $\ind_{m, y}$ is zero
   881	everywhere except for when $x = y$.
   882	For $a\in \F_q^M$, label the coordinates of $a$ as $a_y$ for $y\in \{0,1\}^m$
   883	(identifying the latter set with $\{1,\ldots,M\}$ using, say, the lexicographic
   884	ordering on strings).
   885	For any such $a$ define the multilinear polynomial $g_a: \F_q^m \to \F_q$,
   886	called the \emph{low-degree encoding of $a$}, as follows:
   887	\begin{equation}
   888	\label{eq:ld-encoding}
   889		 g_a(x) = \sum_{y \in \{0,1\}^m} a_y \cdot \ind_{m,y}(x)\;.
   890	\end{equation}
   891	Note that for any $y \in \{0,1\}^m$, $g_a(y) = a_y$.
   892	Furthermore, the map $a\mapsto g_a$ is linear: for every $x \in \F_q^m$,
   893	\begin{equation}
   894	\label{eq:low-degree-encoding-definition}
   895		g_a(x) = a \cdot \ind_m(x)\;,
   896	\end{equation}
   897	where $\ind_m(x)$ is the vector $(\ind_{m,y}(x))_{y \in \{0,1\}^m}\in\F_q^M$.
   898	
   899	\begin{lemma}
   900	\label{lem:ld-encoding-complexity}
   901	Let $q$ be an admissible field size, and let $M = 2^m$ for some integer $m$.
   902	The complexity of computing the evaluation of the low-degree encoding $g_a(x)$,
   903	given $a \in \F_q^M$ and $x \in \F_q^m$ represented in binary, is $\poly(M,\log
   904	q)$.
   905	\end{lemma}
   906	\begin{proof}
   907		Computing $g_a(x)$ requires computing the sum of products $a_y \cdot
   908	  \ind_{m,y}(x)$ over all $y \in \{0,1\}^m$.
   909	  Via \Cref{lem:efficient_arithmetic}, evaluating $\ind_{m,y}(x)$ takes time
   910	  $\poly(m,\log q)$ because it requires performing $m$ multiplications of $\F_q$
   911	  elements, and therefore the product $a_y \cdot \ind_{m,y}(x)$ requires
   912	  $\poly(m,\log q)$ time.
   913	  Computing the sum over all $y \in \{0,1\}^m$ requires $M \cdot \poly(m,\log q)
   914	  = \poly(M,\log q)$ time, as claimed.
   915	\end{proof}
   916	
   917	Finally, for any $H \subseteq \F_q$ we define the \emph{decoding} map
   918	$\coded_H(\cdot)$ which takes as input a polynomial $g : \F_q^m \to \F_q$ and
   919	returns the following vector $a \in \F_q^M$: for all $y \in \{0,1\}^m$, if $g(y)
   920	\in H$, then set $a_y = g(y)$, and otherwise set $a_y = 0$.
   921	Note that for all $a \in H^M$ we have $\coded_H(g_a) = a$ where $g_a$ is the
   922	low-degree encoding of $a$.
   923	For notational brevity we often write $\coded(\cdot)$ to denote the boolean
   924	decoding map $\coded_{\{0,1\}}(\cdot)$.

     4	/-!
     5	# Pauli basis test soundness interface
     6	
     7	This module contains the quantitative error function and the closed definitions
     8	used to state Pauli basis test soundness.  The carriers are concrete
     9	finite-dimensional vectors and matrices so that the soundness proof can use the
    10	existing Hilbert-space API without introducing a dependency cycle.
    11	
    12	## References
    13	
    14	The interface supports `thm:pauli` in
    15	`blueprint/src/chapter/ch13_qpbt_test.tex:407-424`, with paper origin
    16	`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:1426-1447`.
    17	The distance functionals use `def:state-distance` and `def:povm-distance` from
    18	`blueprint/src/chapter/ch12_qpbt_games.tex:187-226`.

    24

    26	open MIPStarRE.Quantum

    30	/-- The Pauli-test error scale.  The argument order is `(a, b, ε, m, d, q)`;
    31	the powers are real `rpow`s and the asymptotic constants are absorbed into `a`,
    32	as specified by `thm:pauli` (`blueprint/src/chapter/ch13_qpbt_test.tex:407-424`,
    33	paper `references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:1426-1447`).
    34	-/
    35	noncomputable def deltaQld (a b ε : ℝ) (m d q : ℕ) : ℝ :=
    36	  a * Real.rpow ((m * d : ℕ) : ℝ) a *
    37	    (Real.rpow ε b + Real.rpow (q : ℝ) (-b) +
    38	      Real.rpow 2 (-(b * ((m * d : ℕ) : ℝ))))
    39	
    40	/-- Monotonicity obligation for adjusting the universal constants in
    41	`deltaQld` on the source parameter domain. This Lean-only helper supports the
    42	enlargement of `a` and shrinkage of `b` for `0 ≤ ε ≤ 1` described in the
    43	Chapter 16 preamble (`blueprint/src/chapter/ch16_qpbt_extraction.tex:101-104`);
    44	the source makes this constant adjustment at
    45	`references/qpbt-paper/14_analysis_of_the_pauli_basis_test.tex:1402`. It is not
    46	an additional hypothesis of `thm:pauli` or `lem:qld-4-7`. -/
    47	theorem deltaQld_mono {P : AdmissibleParams} {a a' b b' ε : ℝ}
    48	    (ha0 : 1 ≤ a) (ha : a ≤ a') (hb : b' ≤ b) (hb' : 0 < b')
    49	    (hε0 : 0 ≤ ε) (hε1 : ε ≤ 1) :
    50	    deltaQld a b ε P.m P.d P.q ≤ deltaQld a' b' ε P.m P.d P.q := by
    51	  sorry
    52	
    53	/-- The ideal auxiliary state `aux ⊗ EPR_q^{⊗M}` in the shuffled register
    54	ordering.  The EPR factor is the concrete `eprState` from
    55	`def:EPR` (`blueprint/src/chapter/ch11_qpbt_algebra.tex:537-547`; paper
    56	`references/qpbt-paper/04_preliminaries.tex:946-955`).
    57	-/
    58	noncomputable def idealState (P : AdmissibleParams)
    59	    {ιA' ιB' : Type*} [Fintype ιA'] [DecidableEq ιA']
    60	    [Fintype ιB'] [DecidableEq ιB']
    61	    (aux : EuclideanSpace ℂ (ιA' × ιB')) :
    62	    EuclideanSpace ℂ ((ιA' × PauliRegister P) × (ιB' × PauliRegister P)) :=
    63	  (EuclideanSpace.equiv ((ιA' × PauliRegister P) ×
    64	      (ιB' × PauliRegister P)) ℂ).symm
    65	    (fun p =>
    66	      ((EuclideanSpace.equiv (ιA' × ιB') ℂ) aux (p.1.1, p.2.1)) *
    67	        ((EuclideanSpace.equiv (PauliRegister P × PauliRegister P) ℂ)
    68	          (eprState (PauliRegister P)) (p.1.2, p.2.2)))
    69	
    70	/-- The A-side ideal Pauli projector, with identities on the auxiliary and
    71	B-side registers.  This is a concrete matrix form of the operator comparison
    72	in `thm:pauli` (`blueprint/src/chapter/ch13_qpbt_test.tex:407-424`; paper
    73	`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:1426-1447`).
    74	-/
    75	noncomputable def pauliProjOnA'' (P : AdmissibleParams)
    76	    {ιA' ιB' : Type*} [Fintype ιA'] [DecidableEq ιA']
    77	    [Fintype ιB'] [DecidableEq ιB'] (W : PauliKind)
    78	    (u : PauliRegister P) :
    79	    Op ((ιA' × PauliRegister P) × (ιB' × PauliRegister P)) :=
    80	  fun p q =>
    81	    if p.1.1 = q.1.1 ∧ p.2 = q.2 then

    86	`ch13_qpbt_test.tex:407-424`, paper origin

    95	    if p.1 = q.1 ∧ p.2.1 = q.2.1 then

   116	blueprint `ch13_qpbt_test.tex:407-424`, paper origin

   119	noncomputable def liftedBEffect {P : AdmissibleParams} {G : Game}
   120	    (S : Strategy G) {ιA' ιB' : Type*} [Fintype ιA'] [DecidableEq ιA']
   121	    [Fintype ιB'] [DecidableEq ιB']
   122	    (φB : EuclideanSpace ℂ S.ιB →ₗᵢ[ℂ]
   123	      EuclideanSpace ℂ (ιB' × PauliRegister P))
   124	    (M : Op S.ιB) :
   125	    Op ((ιA' × PauliRegister P) × (ιB' × PauliRegister P)) :=
   126	  fun p q =>
   127	    if p.1 = q.1 then
   128	      (conjIsometry φB M) p.2 q.2
   129	    else 0

   131	/-- A finite witness packaging the auxiliary dimensions, isometries, and state
   132	from `thm:pauli`.  This structure is a Lean-only encoding of the existential
   133	data in the paper theorem; it introduces no extra hypothesis.  Blueprint

   142	  [ιBFintype : Fintype ιB']
   143	  [ιADecidableEq : DecidableEq ιA']
   144	  [ιBDecidableEq : DecidableEq ιB']
   145	  φA : EuclideanSpace ℂ S.ιA →ₗᵢ[ℂ]
   146	    EuclideanSpace ℂ (ιA' × PauliRegister P)

   148	    EuclideanSpace ℂ (ιB' × PauliRegister P)

    31	abbrev SixReg (P : AdmissibleParams) (ιA ιB : Type*) :=
    32	  (ιA × (PauliRegister P × PauliRegister P)) ×
    33	    (ιB × (PauliRegister P × PauliRegister P))
    34	
    35	/-- Equality of six-register indices is supplied by classical decidability for
    36	the register type. This is the index set of `def:expanded-state`; blueprint
    37	`ch14_qpbt_observables.tex:760-781`. -/
    38	noncomputable instance sixRegDecidableEq (P : AdmissibleParams)
    39	    (ιA ιB : Type*) : DecidableEq (SixReg P ιA ιB) :=
    40	  Classical.decEq _
    41	
    42	/-- Reassociate the tensor product of the strategy state and two EPR states
    43	directly into register order `AA'A''BB'B''` for
    44	`eq:def-psihat`, paper `14_analysis_of_the_pauli_basis_test.tex:367-372`. -/
    45	def sixRegShuffle (P : AdmissibleParams) (ιA ιB : Type*) :
    46	    (((ιA × ιB) × (PauliRegister P × PauliRegister P)) ×
    47	        (PauliRegister P × PauliRegister P)) ≃ SixReg P ιA ιB where
    48	  toFun p := ((p.1.1.1, (p.1.2.1, p.1.2.2)),
    49	    (p.1.1.2, (p.2.1, p.2.2)))
    50	  invFun p := (((p.1.1, p.2.1), (p.1.2.1, p.1.2.2)),
    51	    (p.2.2.1, p.2.2.2))
    52	  left_inv p := by cases p; rfl
    53	  right_inv p := by cases p; rfl
    54	
    55	/-- The four placements `AA'`, `BA''`, `BB'`, and `AB''` used explicitly in
    56	the chapter-14 consistency statements. Paper
    57	`14_analysis_of_the_pauli_basis_test.tex:420-450`; blueprint
    58	`ch14_qpbt_observables.tex:876-922`. -/
    59	inductive Placement where
    60	  | AA'
    61	  | BA''
    62	  | BB'
    63	  | AB''
    64	  deriving DecidableEq, Repr, Inhabited, Fintype
    65	
    66	/-- The strategy-player side supplying the local Hilbert space in each of the
    67	four register placements at paper
    68	`14_analysis_of_the_pauli_basis_test.tex:420-450`. -/
    69	def Placement.side : Placement → PlayerSide
    70	  | .AA' => .alice
    71	  | .BA'' => .bob
    72	  | .BB' => .bob
    73	  | .AB'' => .alice
    74	
    75	namespace ProjectiveSetting
    76	
    77	variable {P : AdmissibleParams} {ε : ℝ}
    78	
    79	/-- A strategy-local register paired with one generalized-Pauli register. This
    80	is the operator space in `def:expanded-observables`, paper
    81	`14_analysis_of_the_pauli_basis_test.tex:374-382`. -/
    82	abbrev ExpandedLocalSpace (S : ProjectiveSetting P ε) (side : PlayerSide) :=
    83	  S.LocalSpace side × PauliRegister P
    84	
    85	/-- The strategy state tensored with EPR states on `A'A''` and `B'B''`, in the
    86	six-register order. This is `eq:def-psihat`, paper
    87	`14_analysis_of_the_pauli_basis_test.tex:367-372`, blueprint
    88	`ch14_qpbt_observables.tex:760-781`. -/
    89	noncomputable def psiHat (S : ProjectiveSetting P ε) :
    90	    EuclideanSpace ℂ (SixReg P S.toStrategy.ιA S.toStrategy.ιB) := by
    91	  classical
    92	  exact
    93	    reindexState (sixRegShuffle P S.toStrategy.ιA S.toStrategy.ιB)
    94	      (vecTensor
    95	        (vecTensor S.toStrategy.ψ (eprState (PauliRegister P)))
    96	        (eprState (PauliRegister P)))
    97	
    98	/-- Place an operator on one of `AA'`, `BA''`, `BB'`, or `AB''`, with the
    99	identity on all remaining registers. The input local space is determined by
   100	the placement, so no equality between the player spaces is assumed. Paper
   101	`14_analysis_of_the_pauli_basis_test.tex:420-450`; blueprint
   102	`ch14_qpbt_observables.tex:876-922`. -/
   103	noncomputable def place (S : ProjectiveSetting P ε) (p : Placement)
   104	    (O : Op (S.ExpandedLocalSpace p.side)) :
   105	    Op (SixReg P S.toStrategy.ιA S.toStrategy.ιB) :=
   106	  fun i j =>
   107	    match p with
   108	    | .AA' =>
   109	        O (i.1.1, i.1.2.1) (j.1.1, j.1.2.1) *
   110	          (1 : Op (PauliRegister P)) i.1.2.2 j.1.2.2 *
   111	          (1 : Op S.toStrategy.ιB) i.2.1 j.2.1 *
   112	          (1 : Op (PauliRegister P)) i.2.2.1 j.2.2.1 *
   113	          (1 : Op (PauliRegister P)) i.2.2.2 j.2.2.2
   114	    | .BA'' =>
   115	        (1 : Op S.toStrategy.ιA) i.1.1 j.1.1 *
   116	          (1 : Op (PauliRegister P)) i.1.2.1 j.1.2.1 *
   117	          O (i.2.1, i.1.2.2) (j.2.1, j.1.2.2) *
   118	          (1 : Op (PauliRegister P)) i.2.2.1 j.2.2.1 *
   119	          (1 : Op (PauliRegister P)) i.2.2.2 j.2.2.2
   120	    | .BB' =>
   121	        (1 : Op S.toStrategy.ιA) i.1.1 j.1.1 *
   122	          (1 : Op (PauliRegister P)) i.1.2.1 j.1.2.1 *
   123	          (1 : Op (PauliRegister P)) i.1.2.2 j.1.2.2 *
   124	          O (i.2.1, i.2.2.1) (j.2.1, j.2.2.1) *
   125	          (1 : Op (PauliRegister P)) i.2.2.2 j.2.2.2
   126	    | .AB'' =>
   127	        O (i.1.1, i.2.2.2) (j.1.1, j.2.2.2) *
   128	          (1 : Op (PauliRegister P)) i.1.2.1 j.1.2.1 *
   129	          (1 : Op (PauliRegister P)) i.1.2.2 j.1.2.2 *
   130	          (1 : Op S.toStrategy.ιB) i.2.1 j.2.1 *
   131	          (1 : Op (PauliRegister P)) i.2.2.1 j.2.2.1
   132	
   133	/-- The expanded observable
   134	`W^r(u) tensor tau^W(r * ind_m(u))` on a selected player side. This is
   135	Equation `eq:lc-23`, paper `14_analysis_of_the_pauli_basis_test.tex:374-382`,
   136	blueprint `ch14_qpbt_observables.tex:783-807`. -/
   137	noncomputable def expObs (S : ProjectiveSetting P ε) (side : PlayerSide)
   138	    (W : PauliKind) (r : PauliScalar P) (u : Fin P.m → PauliScalar P) :
   139	    Op (S.ExpandedLocalSpace side) :=
   140	  heteroKron (S.pointObs side W r u)
   141	    (tauObservable W (fun h => r * indicatorVec u h))
   142	
   143	/-- The Fourier average defining the expanded point effect. This is the first
   144	display of `def:expanded-point-measurement`, paper
   145	`14_analysis_of_the_pauli_basis_test.tex:384-418`, blueprint
   146	`ch14_qpbt_observables.tex:809-844`. -/
   147	noncomputable def expPointOp (S : ProjectiveSetting P ε) (side : PlayerSide)
   148	    (W : PauliKind) (u : Fin P.m → PauliScalar P) (a : PauliScalar P) :
   149	    Op (S.ExpandedLocalSpace side) :=
   150	  averageOperatorOverDistribution (uniformDistribution (PauliScalar P)) fun r =>
   151	    phaseSign (fixedBinTrace P.model (a * r)) • S.expObs side W r u
   152	
   153	/-- The Pauli-register projector onto labels whose low-degree encoding has
   154	value `a` at `u`. This is Equation `eq:qld-point-obs-def`, paper
   155	`14_analysis_of_the_pauli_basis_test.tex:389-394`, blueprint
   156	`ch14_qpbt_observables.tex:809-844`. -/
   157	noncomputable def tauPointProj (W : PauliKind)
   158	    (u : Fin P.m → PauliScalar P) (a : PauliScalar P) : Op (PauliRegister P) :=
   159	  ∑ h ∈ Finset.univ.filter (fun h : PauliRegister P =>
   160	      dotProduct h (indicatorVec u) = a),
   161	    pauliProj W h
   162	
   163	/-- Expanded point effects are positive semidefinite. This is the positivity
   164	obligation in `def:expanded-point-measurement`, paper
   165	`14_analysis_of_the_pauli_basis_test.tex:384-418`. -/
   166	theorem expPointOp_nonneg (S : ProjectiveSetting P ε) (side : PlayerSide)
   167	    (W : PauliKind) (u : Fin P.m → PauliScalar P) (a : PauliScalar P) :
   168	    0 ≤ S.expPointOp side W u a := by
   169	  sorry
   170	
   171	/-- Expanded point effects sum to the identity. This is the completeness
   172	obligation in `def:expanded-point-measurement`, paper
   173	`14_analysis_of_the_pauli_basis_test.tex:384-418`. -/
   174	theorem expPointOp_sum_eq_one (S : ProjectiveSetting P ε) (side : PlayerSide)
   175	    (W : PauliKind) (u : Fin P.m → PauliScalar P) :
   176	    ∑ a, S.expPointOp side W u a = 1 := by
   177	  sorry
   178	
   179	/-- The complete expanded point measurement on the chosen player and Pauli
   180	register. Its effects are those of `def:expanded-point-measurement`, paper
   181	`14_analysis_of_the_pauli_basis_test.tex:384-418`, blueprint
   182	`ch14_qpbt_observables.tex:809-844`. -/
   183	noncomputable def pointMeasExp (S : ProjectiveSetting P ε) (side : PlayerSide)
   184	    (W : PauliKind) (u : Fin P.m → PauliScalar P) :
   185	    Measurement (PauliScalar P) (S.ExpandedLocalSpace side) :=
   186	  Measurement.ofSumEqOne (S.expPointOp side W u)
   187	    (S.expPointOp_nonneg side W u) (S.expPointOp_sum_eq_one side W u)
   188	
   189	/-- The expanded point effect is the convolution of the strategy point
   190	measurement and the Pauli-register point projection. This is the final display
   191	of `def:expanded-point-measurement`, paper
   192	`14_analysis_of_the_pauli_basis_test.tex:395-418`. -/
   193	theorem expPointOp_eq_convolution (S : ProjectiveSetting P ε)
   194	    (side : PlayerSide) (W : PauliKind) (u : Fin P.m → PauliScalar P)
   195	    (a : PauliScalar P) :
   196	    S.expPointOp side W u a =
   197	      ∑ p ∈ Finset.univ.filter (fun p : PauliScalar P × PauliScalar P =>
   198	          p.1 + p.2 = a),
   199	        heteroKron ((S.pointMeas side W u).effect p.1)
   200	          (tauPointProj W u p.2) := by
   201	  sorry
   202	
   203	/-- The expanded point measurement is projective, as asserted after the
   204	convolution formula in `def:expanded-point-measurement`, paper
   205	`14_analysis_of_the_pauli_basis_test.tex:395-418`. -/
   206	theorem pointMeasExp_isProjective (S : ProjectiveSetting P ε)
   207	    (side : PlayerSide) (W : PauliKind) (u : Fin P.m → PauliScalar P) :
   208	    MIPStarRE.QPBT.Measurement.IsProjective (S.pointMeasExp side W u) := by
   209	  sorry
   210	
   211	/-- Trace-coarse-graining of the expanded point measurement. This is Equation
   212	`eq:qld-def-mptur`, paper `14_analysis_of_the_pauli_basis_test.tex:411-418`,
   213	blueprint `ch14_qpbt_observables.tex:846-874`. -/
   214	noncomputable def expPointTrace (S : ProjectiveSetting P ε)
   215	    (side : PlayerSide) (W : PauliKind) (u : Fin P.m → PauliScalar P)
   216	    (r : PauliScalar P) : Measurement (ZMod 2) (S.ExpandedLocalSpace side) :=
   217	  (S.pointMeasExp side W u).postprocess fun a => fixedBinTrace P.model (a * r)
   218	
   219	/-- Fourier inversion writes a trace-coarse-grained point effect as one half
   220	of the identity plus its signed expanded observable. This is Equation
   221	`eq:lc-22`, paper `14_analysis_of_the_pauli_basis_test.tex:411-418`, blueprint
   222	`ch14_qpbt_observables.tex:846-874`. -/
   223	theorem expPointTrace_eq_half_add (S : ProjectiveSetting P ε)
   224	    (side : PlayerSide) (W : PauliKind) (u : Fin P.m → PauliScalar P)
   225	    (r : PauliScalar P) (b : ZMod 2) :
   226	    (S.expPointTrace side W u r).effect b =
   227	      (2 : ℂ)⁻¹ •
   228	        (1 + phaseSign b • S.expObs side W r u) := by
   229	  sorry
   230	
   231	end ProjectiveSetting
   232	
   233	end
   234	
   235	end MIPStarRE.QPBT

     3	/-!
     4	# Quantitative state and operator distances
     5	
     6	The blueprint uses asymptotic `approx` notation.  The skeleton records the
     7	corresponding squared norm functionals explicitly, leaving universal-constant
     8	estimates to later proof stages.
     9	
    10	## References
    11	
    12	These are `def:state-distance` and `def:povm-distance` in
    13	`blueprint/src/chapter/ch12_qpbt_games.tex:171-220`; the paper origin is
    14	`references/qpbt-paper/06_nonlocal_games_and_mipstar.tex:219-271`.
    15	-/
    16	
    17	open scoped BigOperators
    18	
    19	namespace MIPStarRE.QPBT
    20	
    21	open MIPStarRE.LDT
    22	open MIPStarRE.Quantum
    23	
    24	/--
    25	Squared Euclidean distance between pure states.  Blueprint `def:state-distance`
    26	(`blueprint/src/chapter/ch12_qpbt_games.tex:171-179`), paper origin
    27	`references/qpbt-paper/06_nonlocal_games_and_mipstar.tex:219-271`.
    28	-/
    29	noncomputable def stateDistSq {ι : Type*} [Fintype ι]
    30	    [DecidableEq ι]
    31	    (ψ φ : EuclideanSpace ℂ ι) : ℝ :=
    32	  ‖ψ - φ‖ ^ 2
    33	
    34	/--
    35	Average squared state-dependent distance between two operator families.  This
    36	is `def:povm-distance` in `blueprint/src/chapter/ch12_qpbt_games.tex:203-210`,
    37	with paper origin `references/qpbt-paper/06_nonlocal_games_and_mipstar.tex:219-271`.
    38	-/
    39	noncomputable def opFamilyDistSq {X α ι : Type*}
    40	    [Fintype α] [Fintype ι] [DecidableEq ι]
    41	    (μ : Distribution X) (M N : X → α → Op ι)
    42	    (ψ : EuclideanSpace ℂ ι) : ℝ :=
    43	  avgOver μ (fun x =>
    44	    ∑ a : α, ‖applyOperatorToState (M x a - N x a) ψ‖ ^ 2)
    45	
    46	end MIPStarRE.QPBT

     4	/-!
     5	# Polynomial combination and restricted line distributions
     6	
     7	This file contains the concrete definitions at the foundation of the
     8	Chapter 15 combining argument.  A pair of bounded individual-degree
     9	polynomials is embedded into the two coordinate blocks of an extended
    10	polynomial.  On lines, explicit affine reparameterizations are composed with
    11	coefficient-list polynomials.  The original-dimensional restricted line laws
    12	are formed before decoding, while their field seed is still present.
    13	
    14	## References
    15	
    16	The combining map is `def:combine-map` in
    17	`blueprint/src/chapter/ch15_qpbt_combining.tex:445-480`, with paper origin
    18	`references/qpbt-paper/14_analysis_of_the_pauli_basis_test.tex:970-989`.
    19	The restricted laws are `def:ith-restricted-line` in blueprint lines 578--592,
    20	with paper origin in the same source at lines 1038--1048.
    21	-/
    22	
    23	open scoped BigOperators
    24	
    25	namespace MIPStarRE.QPBT
    26	
    27	open MIPStarRE.LDT
    28	open MIPStarRE.LDT.Preliminaries
    29	
    30	noncomputable section
    31	
    32	/-- The bounded individual-degree polynomial outcome used by the global
    33	pair measurement.  This is the actual `polyFunc` subtype from
    34	`def:polyfunc`, not a coefficient-box replacement. -/
    35	noncomputable abbrev Poly (P : AdmissibleParams) :=
    36	  ↥(MIPStarRE.LDT.Preliminaries.polyFunc P.m (PauliScalar P) P.d)
    37	
    38	/-- Pairs of bounded polynomial representatives returned by the global
    39	measurement in `lem:qld-4-7`. -/
    40	noncomputable abbrev PolyPair (P : AdmissibleParams) := Poly P × Poly P
    41	
    42	/-- Split the extended coordinate set into the `X` block, the `Z` block, and
    43	the two scalar coordinates.  This is formalization-only coordinate plumbing
    44	for `def:combine-map`, blueprint
    45	`blueprint/src/chapter/ch15_qpbt_combining.tex:445-480`, paper
    46	`references/qpbt-paper/14_analysis_of_the_pauli_basis_test.tex:970-989`. -/
    47	def finCombineEquiv (m : ℕ) :
    48	    Fin (2 * m + 2) ≃ ((Fin m ⊕ Fin m) ⊕ Fin 2) :=
    49	  (finCongr (by omega)).trans
    50	    (finSumFinEquiv.symm.trans
    51	      (Equiv.sumCongr finSumFinEquiv.symm (Equiv.refl (Fin 2))))
    52	
    53	/-- Embed an `X`-block coordinate into the extended coordinate set. -/
    54	def embX (m : ℕ) : Fin m → Fin (2 * m + 2) :=
    55	  fun i => (finCombineEquiv m).symm (.inl (.inl i))
    56	
    57	/-- Embed a `Z`-block coordinate into the extended coordinate set. -/
    58	def embZ (m : ℕ) : Fin m → Fin (2 * m + 2) :=
    59	  fun i => (finCombineEquiv m).symm (.inl (.inr i))
    60	
    61	/-- The extended coordinate occupied by the scalar `alpha`. -/
    62	def alphaVar (m : ℕ) : Fin (2 * m + 2) :=
    63	  (finCombineEquiv m).symm (.inr 0)
    64	
    65	/-- The extended coordinate occupied by the scalar `beta`. -/
    66	def betaVar (m : ℕ) : Fin (2 * m + 2) :=
    67	  (finCombineEquiv m).symm (.inr 1)
    68	
    69	/-- Project an extended point onto its `X` coordinate block. -/
    70	def projX {K : Type*} {m : ℕ} (u : Fin (2 * m + 2) → K) : Fin m → K :=
    71	  fun i => u (embX m i)
    72	
    73	/-- Project an extended point onto its `Z` coordinate block. -/
    74	def projZ {K : Type*} {m : ℕ} (u : Fin (2 * m + 2) → K) : Fin m → K :=
    75	  fun i => u (embZ m i)
    76	
    77	/-- Combine two multivariate polynomials by the formula
    78	`alpha * f(x) + beta * g(z)` from `def:combine-map`.
    79	
    80	Blueprint `blueprint/src/chapter/ch15_qpbt_combining.tex:445-480`; paper
    81	`references/qpbt-paper/14_analysis_of_the_pauli_basis_test.tex:970-983`. -/
    82	noncomputable def combinePoly {K : Type*} [CommSemiring K] {m : ℕ}
    83	    (f g : MvPolynomial (Fin m) K) : MvPolynomial (Fin (2 * m + 2)) K :=
    84	  MvPolynomial.X (alphaVar m) * MvPolynomial.rename (embX m) f +
    85	    MvPolynomial.X (betaVar m) * MvPolynomial.rename (embZ m) g
    86	
    87	/-- Evaluation of `combinePoly` is the displayed combining formula. -/
    88	theorem combinePoly_eval {K : Type*} [CommSemiring K] {m : ℕ}
    89	    (f g : MvPolynomial (Fin m) K) (u : Fin (2 * m + 2) → K) :
    90	    MvPolynomial.eval u (combinePoly f g) =
    91	      u (alphaVar m) * MvPolynomial.eval (projX u) f +
    92	        u (betaVar m) * MvPolynomial.eval (projZ u) g := by
    93	  change MvPolynomial.eval u (combinePoly f g) =
    94	    u (alphaVar m) * MvPolynomial.eval (u ∘ embX m) f +
    95	      u (betaVar m) * MvPolynomial.eval (u ∘ embZ m) g
    96	  simp [combinePoly, MvPolynomial.eval_rename]
    97	
    98	/-- The combining polynomial has individual degree at most `d` when
    99	`hd : 1 ≤ d`.  The coordinate blocks are disjoint: `f` depends only on the
   100	`x` variables and `g` only on the `z` variables, so multiplication by `alpha`
   101	or `beta` preserves the degree bound on those old coordinates and gives degree
   102	one only in the corresponding fresh coordinate.  Thus `hd` supplies exactly
   103	the needed bound on the two fresh coordinates; no `d + 1` bound is introduced.
   104	The statement is the well-definedness assertion in
   105	`def:combine-map`, blueprint
   106	`blueprint/src/chapter/ch15_qpbt_combining.tex:445-480`, with source context
   107	`references/qpbt-paper/14_analysis_of_the_pauli_basis_test.tex:970-983` and the
   108	boundary-hypothesis discussion in `docs/paper-gaps/qpbt_ld-dimension-divisibility.tex`.
   109	-/
   110	theorem combinePoly_mem_polyFunc {K : Type*} [CommSemiring K] {m d : ℕ}
   111	    (hd : 1 ≤ d) {f g : MvPolynomial (Fin m) K}
   112	    (hf : f ∈ polyFunc m K d) (hg : g ∈ polyFunc m K d) :
   113	    combinePoly f g ∈ polyFunc (2 * m + 2) K d := by
   114	  sorry
   115	
   116	/-- Evaluate one member of a global polynomial pair at a point, selecting the
   117	component by Pauli basis.  This is formalization-only support for
   118	`lem:qld-4-7`, paper
   119	`references/qpbt-paper/14_analysis_of_the_pauli_basis_test.tex:1267-1274`. -/
   120	def evalAt {P : AdmissibleParams} (W : PauliKind)
   121	    (u : Fin P.m → PauliScalar P) (pair : PolyPair P) : PauliScalar P :=
   122	  match W with
   123	  | .X => MvPolynomial.eval u pair.1.1
   124	  | .Z => MvPolynomial.eval u pair.2.1
   125	
   126	/-- Interpret a bounded coefficient list as an ordinary univariate
   127	polynomial.  This helper makes the line-combination definition use Mathlib's
   128	actual polynomial composition operation. -/
   129	noncomputable def linePolynomialOfCoefficients {K : Type*} [Semiring K]
   130	    {c : ℕ} (f : Fin (c + 1) → K) : Polynomial K :=
   131	  ∑ i : Fin (c + 1), Polynomial.C (f i) * Polynomial.X ^ i.val
   132	
   133	/-- Evaluating the polynomial represented by a coefficient list agrees with
   134	`evalCoefficient`. -/
   135	theorem linePolynomialOfCoefficients_eval {K : Type*} [Semiring K]
   136	    {c : ℕ} (f : Fin (c + 1) → K) (t : K) :
   137	    (linePolynomialOfCoefficients f).eval t = evalCoefficient f t := by
   138	  change Polynomial.eval t
   139	      (∑ i ∈ Finset.univ, Polynomial.C (f i) * Polynomial.X ^ i.val) =
   140	    ∑ i ∈ Finset.univ, f i * t ^ i.val
   141	  rw [Polynomial.eval_finsetSum]
   142	  simp
   143	
   144	/-- The univariate polynomial before coefficient extraction in
   145	`combineLinePoly`.  The four first scalars describe the affine parameters on
   146	the two projected lines; the last four are the affine `alpha` and `beta`
   147	coordinates of the extended line. -/
   148	noncomputable def combineLinePolynomial {K : Type*} [CommSemiring K] {c : ℕ}
   149	    (aX bX aZ bZ uα vα uβ vβ : K)
   150	    (f g : Fin (c + 1) → K) : Polynomial K :=
   151	  (Polynomial.C uα + Polynomial.C vα * Polynomial.X) *
   152	      (linePolynomialOfCoefficients f).comp
   153	        (Polynomial.C aX + Polynomial.C bX * Polynomial.X) +
   154	    (Polynomial.C uβ + Polynomial.C vβ * Polynomial.X) *
   155	      (linePolynomialOfCoefficients g).comp
   156	        (Polynomial.C aZ + Polynomial.C bZ * Polynomial.X)

   158	/-- The polynomial underlying `combineLinePoly` has degree at most `c + 1`.
   159	This is the degree assertion accompanying Equation `eq:combine-lines` in
   160	`def:combine-map`, blueprint
   161	`blueprint/src/chapter/ch15_qpbt_combining.tex:459-479`, paper
   162	`references/qpbt-paper/14_analysis_of_the_pauli_basis_test.tex:984-989`. -/
   163	theorem combineLinePolynomial_natDegree_le {K : Type*} [CommSemiring K] {c : ℕ}
   164	    (aX bX aZ bZ uα vα uβ vβ : K) (f g : Fin (c + 1) → K) :
   165	    (combineLinePolynomial aX bX aZ bZ uα vα uβ vβ f g).natDegree ≤ c + 1 := by
   166	  sorry

   168	/-- Combine two degree-`c` line polynomials using explicit affine
   169	reparameterizations.  Coefficients through degree `c + 1` are extracted from
   170	the genuine composed polynomial, so the definition has no incompatibility
   171	fallback.
   172	
   173	This is Equation `eq:combine-lines` in `def:combine-map`, blueprint
   174	`blueprint/src/chapter/ch15_qpbt_combining.tex:459-479`, paper
   175	`references/qpbt-paper/14_analysis_of_the_pauli_basis_test.tex:984-989`. -/
   176	noncomputable def combineLinePoly {K : Type*} [CommSemiring K] {c : ℕ}
   177	    (aX bX aZ bZ uα vα uβ vβ : K)
   178	    (f g : Fin (c + 1) → K) : Fin (c + 1 + 1) → K :=
   179	  fun i => (combineLinePolynomial aX bX aZ bZ uα vα uβ vβ f g).coeff i.val
   180	
   181	/-- Compatibility of an extended line with two projected lines and their
   182	explicit affine parameters.  This is precisely the domain condition preceding
   183	Equation `eq:combine-lines`; it is data supplied by the future subline
   184	construction, not a fallback branch in `combineLinePoly`. -/
   185	def IsCombineLineCompatible {K : Type*} [Field K] {m : ℕ}
   186	    (u v : Fin (2 * m + 2) → K)
   187	    (uX vX uZ vZ : Fin m → K)
   188	    (aX bX aZ bZ uα vα uβ vβ : K) : Prop :=
   189	  u (alphaVar m) = uα ∧ v (alphaVar m) = vα ∧
   190	    u (betaVar m) = uβ ∧ v (betaVar m) = vβ ∧
   191	    ∀ t : K,
   192	      projX (u + t • v) = uX + (aX + bX * t) • vX ∧
   193	        projZ (u + t • v) = uZ + (aZ + bZ * t) • vZ
   194	
   195	/-- Under explicit line compatibility, `combineLinePoly` satisfies the
   196	advertised line equation and the two projected points have the stated affine
   197	parameters.  This is the specification obligation for Equation
   198	`eq:combine-lines`, blueprint
   199	`blueprint/src/chapter/ch15_qpbt_combining.tex:459-479`, paper
   200	`references/qpbt-paper/14_analysis_of_the_pauli_basis_test.tex:984-989`. -/
   201	theorem combineLinePoly_spec {K : Type*} [Field K] {m c : ℕ}
   202	    (u v : Fin (2 * m + 2) → K) (uX vX uZ vZ : Fin m → K)
   203	    (aX bX aZ bZ uα vα uβ vβ : K) (f g : Fin (c + 1) → K)
   204	    (hcompat : IsCombineLineCompatible u v uX vX uZ vZ
   205	      aX bX aZ bZ uα vα uβ vβ) :
   206	    ∀ t : K,
   207	      projX (u + t • v) = uX + (aX + bX * t) • vX ∧
   208	      projZ (u + t • v) = uZ + (aZ + bZ * t) • vZ ∧
   209	      evalCoefficient
   210	          (combineLinePoly aX bX aZ bZ uα vα uβ vβ f g) t =
   211	        (uα + t * vα) * evalCoefficient f (aX + bX * t) +
   212	          (uβ + t * vβ) * evalCoefficient g (aZ + bZ * t) := by
   213	  sorry

   251	/-- The normalized pre-decoding axis law conditioned on coordinate `i`. -/
   252	noncomputable def restrictedALinePreDist (L : LdParams) (i : Fin L.m) :

   260	noncomputable def restrictedDLinePreDist (L : LdParams) (i : Fin L.m) :
   261	    Distribution (LdSpace L × LdSpace L) :=
   262	  Distribution.restrict
   263	    (clDistribution (ldDLineCL L) (ldPointCL L))

   265	    (restrictedDLineSeedEvent_positive L i)

     7	/-!
     8	# Witnesses for combining the Pauli bases
     9	
    10	This module defines the five measurement and distribution witnesses used in
    11	the combining argument.  Every measurement is indexed by the player side, so
    12	Alice's and Bob's local spaces remain distinct.  The extended-dimensional
    13	line objects use the directly indexed low-degree interface and therefore do
    14	not require a dimension-divisibility hypothesis.
    15	
    16	## References
    17	
    18	The witnesses formalize `lem:qld-4-10`, `lem:qld-xz-lines`,
    19	`lem:qld-sublines`, `lem:qld-4-13`, and `lem:qld-4-7` in
    20	`blueprint/src/chapter/ch15_qpbt_combining.tex`.  Their paper source is
    21	`references/qpbt-paper/14_analysis_of_the_pauli_basis_test.tex:689-709,
    22	882-894,1020-1069,1267-1274`.
    23	-/

    31	/-! ## The canonical scalar identification -/
    32	
    33	/-- Identify the direct extended game's scalar field with the Pauli scalar
    34	field.  Both are selected by `fixedFieldModel`; only their proof argument for
    35	admissibility differs. -/
    36	noncomputable def extendedDirectScalarEquiv (P : AdmissibleParams) :
    37	    DirectScalarQ P.extendedDirectLd ≃+* PauliScalar P := by
    38	  have h : P.extendedDirectLd.hq = P.hq := Subsingleton.elim _ _
    39	  cases h
    40	  exact RingEquiv.refl _
    41	
    42	/-- Transport an extended direct point into the canonical Pauli scalar field. -/
    43	def directPointToPauli (P : AdmissibleParams)
    44	    (u : Fin P.extendedDirectLd.m -> DirectScalarQ P.extendedDirectLd) :
    45	    Fin (2 * P.m + 2) -> PauliScalar P :=
    46	  fun i => extendedDirectScalarEquiv P (u i)

    48	/-! ## Finite direct-line carrier -/
    49	
    50	/-- A finite code for directly indexed lines, omitting only proof fields. -/
    51	private abbrev DirectLineDescCode (D : DirectLdParams) :=
    52	  ((Fin D.m -> DirectScalarQ D) × Fin D.m) ⊕
    53	    ((Fin D.m -> DirectScalarQ D) × Fin D.m ×
    54	      (Fin D.m -> DirectScalarQ D))
    55	
    56	/-- Encode a directly indexed line by its tag and mathematical data. -/
    57	private def directLineDescCode (D : DirectLdParams) :
    58	    DirectLineDesc D -> DirectLineDescCode D
    59	  | .axis base index _ => .inl (base, index)
    60	  | .diagonal base index direction _ _ => .inr (base, index, direction)
    61	
    62	/-- The direct-line code is injective by proof irrelevance. -/
    63	private theorem directLineDescCode_injective (D : DirectLdParams) :
    64	    Function.Injective (directLineDescCode D) := by
    65	  intro line line' h
    66	  cases line with
    67	  | axis base index baseFixed =>
    68	      cases line' with
    69	      | axis base' index' baseFixed' =>
    70	          simp only [directLineDescCode, Sum.inl.injEq, Prod.mk.injEq] at h
    71	          rcases h with ⟨rfl, rfl⟩
    72	          rfl
    73	      | diagonal => simp [directLineDescCode] at h
    74	  | diagonal base index direction baseFixed prefixZero =>
    75	      cases line' with
    76	      | axis => simp [directLineDescCode] at h
    77	      | diagonal base' index' direction' baseFixed' prefixZero' =>
    78	          simp only [directLineDescCode, Sum.inr.injEq, Prod.mk.injEq] at h
    79	          rcases h with ⟨rfl, rfl, rfl⟩
    80	          rfl
    81	
    82	/-- Directly indexed line descriptions form a finite type. -/
    83	noncomputable instance directLineDescFintype (D : DirectLdParams) :
    84	    Fintype (DirectLineDesc D) :=
    85	  Fintype.ofInjective (directLineDescCode D) (directLineDescCode_injective D)
